transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?

I’m scared that if I start eating more, I’ll lose control and put on weight I can’t afford at my age and in my line of work. My doctor insisted I come in for an evaluation after my last physical, but I just can't risk letting myself get soft.
Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'losing control' when it comes to eating, and how you currently manage your food intake to maintain your weight?

Losing control means breaking my discipline and getting soft or sloppy, which I feel I can't afford now that my wife isn't here to help me keep my life together. To prevent that, I usually get by on just black coffee in the morning and a small piece of chicken or an apple late at night. I avoid full plates entirely and tell the guys at the station I've already eaten so I don't break my routine.
Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and losing control over your eating affects your daily life and relationships, beyond just your professional concerns?

It’s really isolated me, and my sisters are constantly complaining because I barely show up to family gatherings anymore. I get too anxious about eating around other people and having to answer questions about why I'm not eating the traditional Mexican dishes they make. It's just easier to stay away, even though it has put a real strain on our relationship.
Do you often check your body weight or shape, or engage in specific behaviors like excessive exercise to maintain your current weight?

I constantly check the scale and look in the mirror, but I don't see a thin man; I just see a gut and flabby arms that I'm terrified of letting get any bigger. I don't do extreme workouts, but I focus heavily on tightening up my body to stay fit for duty. That means constantly checking how my uniform fits and punching extra holes in my duty belt to make sure I'm not getting sloppy.
Do you believe your weight or body shape is actually normal, but you're afraid of it changing, or do you genuinely see yourself as overweight even when others might not agree?

I genuinely do not see a skinny man when I look in the mirror; even though my pants are hanging off me and I've had to punch extra holes in my duty belt, I still see a gut and flabby arms. Seeing that makes me feel like a complete failure as a cop and as a man. Keeping that number on the scale down is the only way I feel I can stop myself from getting sloppy.
Can you tell me more about what specifically you see when you look in the mirror that makes you think you have a gut and flabby arms, despite others possibly perceiving you as underweight?

Looking in the mirror is incredibly distressing because instead of seeing a thin frame, all I see is a prominent gut and flabby arms. This makes me feel like a complete failure as a cop and as a man who can't keep himself together. Keeping that number on the scale from going up is the only real control I have left in my life right now.

When you imagine yourself gaining weight, what is the worst thing that you think would happen to you, is it more about how you would look and feel about yourself, or is it about the actual health or professional consequences?

It’s really a mix of both. Looking in the mirror and seeing a gut makes me feel like a failure as a man and a cop who is getting "sloppy" like other older guys on the force. At the same time, I have a deep professional fear that gaining weight will make me soft, slow, and useless on the job, especially now that my wife isn't here to help me keep things together.

When you see yourself as having a gut and flabby arms in the mirror, do you think that perception is based on how you actually look, or is it something that your mind is telling you that doesn't match what others see when they look at you?

Even though I know my pants are hanging off me and I've had to punch extra holes in my duty belt, the gut and flabby arms feel completely real to me when I look in the mirror. It's hard to believe it's just my mind playing tricks because what I see makes me feel like such a failure as a cop and a man. I just feel this deep, urgent need to keep that number on the scale from going up.
When you look at other people, do you think they have similar body flaws that you see in yourself, or do you think your body concerns are unique to you?

I haven't really thought about it that way, to be honest. I don't really pay attention to other people's specific flaws; I'm just hyper-focused on my own body. I am just terrified of letting myself get sloppy and losing control.

Do you think your fear of gaining weight and your perception of your body shape would improve if you were to reach a specific weight or body shape goal, or is it more about the fear of losing control over your eating and body regardless of your actual weight?

It’s not about reaching a specific goal weight; there really is no "safe" number for me. It is entirely about the fear of losing control and breaking my discipline. Any increase on the scale triggers a deep fear that I will get soft, sloppy, and completely unable to manage my life without my late wife.

When you're not actively thinking about your weight or body shape, do you still experience significant distress or impairment in your daily life due to physical symptoms or concerns, or is it primarily the fear of gaining weight and losing control that drives your distress?

The distress is primarily driven by that intense fear of putting on weight and losing the only control I have left since my wife passed. I do feel physically weak sometimes, to the point where I've had to turn down physical drills at work, but the real anxiety and the knot in my stomach always come from the thought of getting soft and sloppy.
Can you describe a situation where you felt completely in control of your eating and body shape, and how that differed from your current state of mind?

Before my wife passed away three years ago, I never had to obsess over my eating or body shape because her presence kept our home orderly and balanced out my stressful police work. When she died suddenly, my life felt completely empty and chaotic, which drove me to use strict eating and weight restriction as my only way to feel disciplined and in control.

When you look at pictures of yourself from before your wife passed away, do you see a person with a normal weight and body shape, or do you still perceive flaws in your body even in those older photos?

I don't really look at old photos of myself, and I haven't really thought about how I perceived my body back then. Right now, my focus is entirely on my current weight and shape, and making sure I don't let myself get soft.

Do you believe that if you were to gain a small amount of weight, you would be able to stop worrying about your body shape and feel more in control, or would your fears and anxieties about your weight and body shape persist regardless of any weight gain?

Gaining weight wouldn't ease my worries at all; it would do the exact opposite. Keeping the number on the scale from going up is the only sense of control I have left in my life. Gaining even a small amount would trigger intense anxiety, making me feel like I'm completely losing control, getting soft and sloppy, and failing as a police officer.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight and body shape concerns would decrease if you were unable to weigh yourself or check your body shape in the mirror for an extended period?

I'm not really sure, to be honest, and I haven't ever thought about that. But the idea of not being able to check the scale or look in the mirror actually sounds terrifying and incredibly stressful to me. Those are the only ways I feel I have any real control over my life right now, so losing that would make me feel completely lost.

Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and body shape concerns would change if you were medically required to gain a certain amount of weight for health reasons, such as to undergo a necessary surgery?

I haven't really thought about a scenario like needing surgery, to be honest. But the thought of being forced to gain weight, even for medical reasons, still feels incredibly terrifying to me. It would feel like a complete loss of control, and I just don't think I could handle it.

Do you think your restrictive eating habits are primarily driven by a desire to avoid gaining weight due to a distorted body image, or are they more about a general fear of losing control over your eating and body shape?

It is really a combination of both. When I look in the mirror, I see flabbiness and feel like I'm losing my physical edge as a cop, which makes me feel like a failure. But that is deeply tied to my fear of losing control; restricting food feels like the only way to maintain discipline and order in a life that has been empty and chaotic since my wife passed.

Do you think your fear of gaining weight and body shape concerns would be alleviated if you were able to achieve a sense of control and discipline in your life through means other than restrictive eating and weight management?

In theory, finding other ways to feel in control makes sense, but after losing my wife, my life became so empty and chaotic that it's hard to imagine anything else giving me that same tight grip. Right now, keeping this strict discipline with my eating is the only thing that makes me feel like I have a handle on things. I honestly don't know what else could replace it.

Do you think your fear of gaining weight would decrease if you were able to see yourself as others see you, without the distorted body image you described, or is the fear of gaining weight and losing control more deeply ingrained and independent of your body image concerns?

They are deeply intertwined; while seeing a gut in the mirror drives my anxiety, the fear of getting "soft" and losing control is rooted in the loss of my wife. Controlling my weight feels like the only way I can maintain discipline and keep from falling apart right now. It is a much deeper issue of control that goes far beyond just how I look.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight is more about the actual weight gain itself, or is it about the feeling of losing control and discipline in your life that comes with it?

It is deeply tied to both, but the fear is heavily rooted in losing control and discipline. After my wife passed, my life became empty and chaotic, and controlling my food became the only way to keep from falling apart. Gaining weight feels like the physical manifestation of losing that control, making me feel "soft" and like I'm failing as a cop.

Do you think your distorted body image and fear of gaining weight would improve if you were able to find other sources of control and discipline in your life, or are these fears deeply ingrained regardless of other life circumstances?

Honestly, these fears feel deeply ingrained right now. Ever since my wife passed, controlling my food and weight has been the only thing keeping me from completely falling apart. It’s hard to even imagine what other discipline could replace this, as keeping a tight grip on my body feels like my last line of defense against the chaos of my grief.
Can you describe if there was ever a time when your fear of gaining weight and body shape concerns were absent or less prominent, and what factors contributed to that state?

These fears and body concerns were completely absent before my wife passed away three years ago. When she was alive, she provided an orderly, stable home life that perfectly balanced out the heavy stress of my police work. Because she kept everything together for us, I never felt any need to control my food or obsess over my weight.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight would decrease if you were able to maintain a sense of control and discipline in your eating habits without severely restricting your food intake?

In theory, that sounds logical, but in practice, it is incredibly hard to imagine. Right now, this strict restriction is the only way I know how to feel disciplined, and eating more feels like an automatic loss of control. I'm terrified that relaxing these rules would make me soft and sloppy as a cop, especially since I no longer have my wife to help keep my life together.

Do you believe that your fear of gaining weight is driven more by the potential loss of control and discipline in your life, or by a genuine belief that your body is flawed and needs to be maintained at a certain weight to be acceptable?

It really feels like a mix of both. Keeping strict control over my eating is the only way I feel I can maintain discipline and control in my life after losing my wife. At the same time, when I look in the mirror, I genuinely see a flawed body with a gut and flabby arms that makes me feel like a failure as a cop and a man, so keeping that scale number down is my only grasp on control.

Do you think your distorted body image, where you see a gut and flabby arms despite being underweight, is the primary driver of your restrictive eating habits, or is it the fear of losing control over your life and becoming 'soft' as a cop that drives your need to severely restrict your food intake?

Both are deeply connected, but the primary driver is my desperate need for control. While looking in the mirror and seeing a gut makes me feel like a failure as a cop, restricting food is the only way I feel disciplined after losing my wife. Gaining weight and getting "soft" represents losing that final bit of control over my life.

Do you think you would still feel the need to restrict your food intake if you no longer saw a 'gut' and 'flabby arms' when you looked in the mirror, but still felt like you were in control of your life and your work as a cop?

That’s a tough question, because since my wife passed, my eating, my body, and my sense of control have become completely tangled together. I suppose if I truly felt secure in my life and job and didn't see those flaws in the mirror, the urge to restrict might actually lessen. But right now, it's hard to even imagine that, and restricting is the only tool I have left to feel disciplined and in control.

If you were to regain a sense of control and order in your life through other means, such as therapy or a new support system, do you think your need to restrict food and maintain a certain weight would decrease, or would your fears about body image and weight gain persist?

While regaining some order and support would certainly help with the emptiness since my wife passed, I feel like the fear of gaining weight and looking soft is too deeply ingrained to just disappear. Restricting my food has become my main way of proving to myself that I still have discipline. Even with therapy, I worry that looking in the mirror and seeing myself lose my shape would still make me feel like a failure as a cop and a man.

If you were to see a video or photos of yourself from a third-person perspective, showing your actual body shape and size, do you think that would change your perception of your body and your need to restrict food, or would your fear of gaining weight and losing control persist regardless of this new perspective?

Even if I saw a photo or video of myself from the outside, my deep fear of losing control and gaining weight would absolutely persist. My mind would likely still zero in on any flab or gut and tell me that I'm getting soft and sloppy. The need to maintain strict discipline and control over that scale—especially without my wife here to keep everything together—is just too powerful to be changed by simply looking at a picture.

Do you think your restrictive eating habits and fear of gaining weight would decrease if you were able to find other ways to cope with the emotional emptiness and chaos you've felt since your wife passed away, or are these habits and fears now an integral part of how you define yourself and your sense of discipline?

While this definitely started as a way to cope with the emptiness after my wife passed, it has now become deeply intertwined with my identity and sense of discipline as a cop. The idea of eating more feels like breaking discipline and makes me terrified of becoming soft or sloppy, which feels like the ultimate failure. I'm honestly not sure if finding other coping mechanisms would easily undo how deeply this need for control has taken hold of me.
If you were somehow able to completely eliminate your fear of losing control and discipline, do you think you would still see yourself as having a gut and flabby arms when you look in the mirror?

It’s really hard to separate the two, but even if that fear of losing control were completely gone, the image of a gut and flabby arms in the mirror feels incredibly real and stubborn. Seeing those flaws makes me feel like a failure as a cop and a man, so it is hard to imagine ever seeing myself as "skinny" or being okay with my body. For me, keeping that number on the scale down still feels like the only thing keeping me together.
